elements.text: Windows slightly outperforms macOS and Linux because its implementation is native. Linux can slightly outperform Windows on its native mmap, but that only happens when operating-system wide paging config is manually configured to the scenario. When that is off, even as much as 5% in one case, Linux collapses entirely (grinds to a halt). The behavior must adjust dynamically based on feedback in order to be close to optimal. macOS doesn't even allow manual OS-wide config, and while Linux does it is not sufficient (and not realistic for deployment). There is a slight cost of dynamic adjustment but it's well worth the consistently high performance, lack of pathological collapse, and lack of OS level config.

elements.text:
24GB is the inflection point because of configured hashmap load factor for the 950k chain size (~2.5). This results in table heads totaling 13.6GB. As these must stay memory resident, that leaves 10.4GB for all other processes and table bodies. As this gets squeezed paging increases and time goes parabolic as heads start getting pushed out of RAM. This is a hard point in the store architecture.

LF can be changed via config (only at store create), resulting in smaller heads. Halving the buckets doubles the load factor and therefore the average search cost doubles. So the heads can remain in RAM at 6.8GB while the node pays a more proportional cost in body paging. This of course also has a limit, but as we have shown on the RPi5, it works well at 16GB.

elements.text:
throttle. This operates in the network proxy (the socket encapsulator and base class for all channels). The real work was done in every piece of network code over the past 5 years. Protection operates on backpressure, a design principle I picked up from the late great Pieter Hintjens. So really there's nothing to do except to set a rate limit, so a timer, a handler, and a config setting. The config setting was already in there, and now the rest is done. I will probably also drop in a per service override config setting.

There is no limit whatsoever on how much can be sent to the node/server. The limit is on what we send back. Queries are small, responses are large and costly - and generally the larger the more costly (though not always, so there's some room for tuning this). The interesting part about the handling is that there is no moving window, accumulation or averaging. There's just a rate at which we reply (or notify), in bytes per time.

The send is emitted (at network speed of course), and then the handler invocation is delayed (asynchronously) until the time allocated for that number of bytes is reached. So if the configured rate is faster than network speed, there's no limit. Otherwise the channel is reduced to the configured speed. The total cost is just the timer invocation and its handler indirection, which are trivia in terms of network perf.

elements.text:
Worked all day on getting the Linux mmap up to at least macOS snuff. It looks like that's finally turned the corner. The pivotal issue has been that there is no way to mark a region as retention priority, all you get is global OS config. macOS provide an madvise flag for this, and Windows manages it automatically by observation of access patterns. And hashmap heads need priority retention. The issue has been that they can be accessed much less than bodies, resulting in them getting moved to swap, which is a disaster.

So in the absence of a flag I figured we can just sweep each page with a byte read. No need for any guards, the value is tossed (and the call marked

so that it's not optimized out) and doesn't affect other reads/writes. The cost is low and it keeps the heads more current than the bodies, so cold body pages are released first. That resulted in zero swap (vs. 100% / 8GB). Not done yet, but looking hopeful. This condition arises during validation, milestone had previously been sufficiently optimized.

elements.text: A little piece of debug trivia that I find very interesting, given that we build release with full

A race that corrupts state kills the process with SIGSEGV/SIGBUS on a wild access. noexcept is invisible to that: it governs C++ exception propagation, not signal delivery. The .ips report and any core capture the faulting instruction and all thread stacks regardless.

Here noexcept changes the shape of the dump, in our favor: the throw hits the noexcept boundary and std::terminate fires at the throw site, without unwinding — SIGABRT with the origin frames still on the stack (abort ← terminate ← __cxa_throw ← the actual thrower). In a debug build with NOEXCEPT off, the exception would unwind — and if anything up-stack caught it, the origin would vanish entirely.

So for localization, release-with-noexcept is arguably the better trap.

```A race that corrupts state kills the process with SIGSEGV/SIGBUS on a wild access. noexcept is invisible to that: it governs C++ exception propagation, not signal delivery. The .ips report and any core capture the faulting instruction and all thread stacks regardless.

Here noexcept changes the shape of the dump, in our favor: the throw hits the noexcept boundary and std::terminate fires at the throw site, without unwinding — SIGABRT with the origin frames still on the stack (abort ← terminate ← __cxa_throw ← the actual thrower). In a debug build with NOEXCEPT off, the exception would unwind — and if anything up-stack caught it, the origin would vanish entirely.

So for localization, release-with-noexcept is arguably the better trap.```

text:
Also finally moved the p2p channel into a proper request/response "body" type, so that it can be processed in the socket like all other network protocols. It will now be easy to drop it into http or websockets for example. But more importantly it generalized the implementation, making `bip324` (opportunistic encryption) a clean integration. The p2p protocol is now `p2p/s` with a proper socket variant. I also cleaned up the confusing services configuration settings and integration, which is where p2p privacy is enabled. Still have to do some acceptance testing, but otherwise this is complete.

```[peer]
enable_privacy = true   # new, opportunistic encryption (bip324)
invalid_services = 176  # shitcoins (existing config, retained)
#services_minimum = 42  # obsolete/invalid
#services_maximum = 42  # obsolete/invalid

[node]
# these are new (replace services_minimum/maximum)
limited_blocks  = false
provide_blocks  = true
require_blocks  = true
provide_witness = true
require_witness = true
provide_filters = false```

elements.text: Given that Core is never CPU constrained, this cost does not show up on the wall clock for them at all. But bip324 was promoted as performance neutral and even performance positive due to the removal of the sha256 checksum. That could have been removed without the privacy/encryption - so isn't a genuine argument. But this also ignores the effects of native sha on the checksum computation. On machines with native sha, the checksum is basically free and the encryption therefore is significantly more costly.
"Each v1 P2P message uses a double-SHA256 checksum truncated to 4 bytes. Roughly the same amount of computation power is required for encrypting and authenticating a v2 P2P message as proposed."

Given that Core is never CPU constrained, this cost does not show up on the wall clock for them at all. But bip324 was promoted as performance neutral and even performance positive due to the removal of the sha256 checksum. That could have been removed without the privacy/encryption - so isn't a genuine argument. But this also ignores the effects of native sha on the checksum computation. On machines with native sha, the checksum is basically free and the encryption therefore is significantly more costly.

>  "Each v1 P2P message uses a double-SHA256 checksum truncated to 4 bytes. Roughly the same amount of computation power is required for encrypting and authenticating a v2 P2P message as proposed."

elements.text: Also by default we have the incoming message checksum verification disabled by default (it's a pointless waste of CPU), so if they assumed people kept using that it also throws off their analysis.

elements.text:
The CPU increase was 47%. I optimized the encryption a bit, and vectorized it using our SIMD abstractions. This reduced it to +22% on AVX2, and AVX512 should cut that in half again.

In any case, the continuous encryption is obviously not the free win that the bip324 authors speculated it would be. That was based on assumptions of scalar sha implementation (rare these days) and falsely on the necessity of retaining that message checksum. It's a large amount of additional processing, so if you want max full validation sync speed, leave it off.

The CPU increase was 47%. I optimized the encryption a bit, and vectorized it using our SIMD abstractions. This reduced it to +22% on AVX2, and AVX512 should cut that in half again.

In any case, the continuous encryption is obviously not the free win that the bip324 authors speculated it would be. That was based on assumptions of scalar sha implementation (rare these days) and falsely on the necessity of retaining that message checksum. It's a large amount of additional processing, so if you want max full validation sync speed, leave it off.

elements.text: Benchmarked against the Core implementation. It doesn't vectorize, and in a simple scalar implementation, it's a little faster - though I still have to optimize Poly1305, which should eliminate that. Our network layer over it should also be faster given less allocation and copy of these big (e.g. block) buffers. But with SIMD we are much faster. After normalizing the implementation for 128/256/512 vectorization on Intel/AMD and Arm, to match our hashing templates design, we are now significantly faster than Core across the hardware spectrum, and the above CPU impact should be marginal. More optimizations and benchmarks pending.

elements.text: Core internally returns (query return) the MTP of block N+1 when asked for block N. We never inherited this internal slop, but they actually also emit it on the wire via their json-rpc interface. So when you get the "median time past" with block N, you are actually getting the MTP for block N+1. Something to watch out for when validating the interface.

After some more travel I'm back to it. I previously (8/18-19) cleared these items from the punch list:
```[x] Linux OOM kill at store creation on 8GB (initialize on disk)
[x] restore after height index regress (change to headers)
[x] broken store with no snap should create empty store
[x] restore after prevouts prune (unsafe)
[x] archive immutable store settings in genesis
[x] API from ultrafast to detect GPU usability
[x] milestone prompt when not explicitly configured```
Also as of today, hashmap tables carry an `expected` element count, from which the store derives optimal boom filter k at create (formerly suboptimal), persisted via the settings envelope across load/restore. The bs defaults are recalibrated to a `mainnet 950k` basis: expected element counts, buckets sized for a 2.5 load factor, and minimum body allocations at 1% of the pruned body with 1% growth.

I am continuing to optimize the custom posix mmap implementations, which has resulted in more performance improvement at the low RAM end*. The default allocations and growth rates are dramatically smaller than previous defaults. They no longer have a significant impact on sync performance, and this is a much more flexible configuration. With this done I'll be moving on to default store config automation as a function of available RAM.

(*) e.g. Linux 8 GB RAM mini pruned with full address index now completes a 950k milestone run on 2.5Gbps in `38 minutes`.

Also removed the slab scan (`-a`) command line option, as it has been obsoleted for some time due to a redesign of the ins/points tables. ins and outs are an association record table that each point to inputs and outputs slab tables. So in/out element counts are simply array size.
